title: The Revival, the heart's mirror
hook: the heart is a mirror, dulled by sins and polished by remembrance
tomorrow: bad news and good news in the same hour. now what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, The Revival on fasting: stomach, limbs, and the fast of the heart. Today, the heart itself, and what it's like inside.
screen: `THE FAST OF THE HEART.` → `TODAY, THE HEART ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Step out of a hot shower and the bathroom mirror is a white blur. You can wipe a stripe with your hand and see one eye, then it fogs again. The Qur'an has a picture like that, only darker. Of people who keep doing wrong, it says, in Pickthall's words: "Nay, but that which they have earned is rust upon their hearts." A hadith in at-Tirmidhi explains: each wrong leaves a dark spot on the heart, and turning back to God polishes it clean. So what fogs the mirror is what we do. What clears it?
screen: `A FOGGED BATHROOM MIRROR.` → `RUST UPON THEIR HEARTS.` → `WHAT CLEARS IT?`

segments.voice: Al-Ghazali builds a whole picture on it in the Revival. The heart is a mirror, made to reflect what is true. Wrongdoing dulls it. Remembrance of God, dhikr, polishes it, until it can show things as they really are. So far, everyone agrees. Here's where two teachers in this tradition lean different ways, and both deserve a hearing. One view, which al-Ghazali presses in the Revival: remembrance polishes when the heart is in it. Words on the tongue with a heart somewhere else do little; the polish is the attention. The other view, from Ibn Ata'illah, whose sayings arrive in a few days: don't give up remembrance because you don't feel present in it. Forgetting God altogether is worse than remembering him distractedly, and remembering distractedly can lead to waking up, and waking up to presence. So keep saying the words; the heart may follow. Notice what they share. Neither says the mirror is hopeless. Neither says to stop. One stresses where the polish comes from. The other stresses not putting down the cloth. And the surprising part, which both would sign: a fogged mirror isn't broken. It's a mirror that needs wiping.
screen: `A MIRROR MADE TO REFLECT.` · `ONE VIEW: THE POLISH IS ATTENTION.` · `THE OTHER: DON'T PUT DOWN THE CLOTH.` · `FOGGED ISN'T BROKEN.` · then, large: `THE MIRROR.`

segments.voice: On each out-breath, say one word of remembrance softly: subhanallah, glory be to God. Some breaths your mind will be there and some it won't. Keep the cloth moving either way, one breath, one word, until the bell.
screen: `SUBHANALLAH, ON EACH OUT-BREATH.` · `KEEP THE CLOTH MOVING.`

segments.voice: The Revival, again: here the heart pictured as a mirror, dulled by wrongdoing and polished by remembrance.
Hold this up today: the mirror. Fogged isn't broken, and wiping is allowed to take a while.

howItsDone: Muslims practice dhikr, repeating phrases such as subhanallah, alhamdulillah and astaghfirullah, often on prayer beads, and turn back to God after wrongdoing; Sufi teachers describe this as polishing the heart.

dhikr.meaning: remembrance of God, often repeated short phrases

at-Tirmidhi.meaning: a classical hadith scholar; his collection keeps the dark-spot hadith

Ibn Ata'illah.meaning: a Sufi teacher whose short sayings are called the Hikam

Debate: al-Ghazali (Ihya, book on dhikr) holds that remembrance on the tongue with a heedless heart is of little benefit; Ibn Ata'illah (Hikam; numbered 47 in some editions) says not to abandon dhikr for lack of presence, since heedlessness of dhikr is worse than heedlessness in it, and it may lead to wakefulness, then presence. Confirm both attributions and that the contrast is fair (al-Ghazali also values persistence; the voice says he 'presses' attention, not that he forbids tongue-dhikr).
